items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Electron Release Engineering: A Practical Guide to Versioning, CI Build Matrices, Update Channels, Artifact Integrity, and Safe Rollbacks
items.summary: Shipping a web app mostly means deploying a new build to a server; users load the fresh code on their next request. An Electron release is the opposite: you produce native installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux, each signed and packaged for several architectures, host them somewhere a feed can read, keep update metadata in sync, and then decide which users actually move to which version. When something goes wrong, the fix is not a redeploy of one bundle — it is withdrawing or blocking a native build that may already be installed on thousands of machines. Release engineering for Electron is the layer between "the code works on my laptop" and "a built artifact can be safely signed, shipped, updated, and rolled back across platforms." This guide covers a single source of truth for version numbers, a CI build matrix that handles the platform and architecture combinations, where signing and notarization belong as gates, what update metadata actually contains, how release channels separate beta and stable audiences, how changelogs are generated from history, how artifact integrity is verified, and how to plan a rollback before you need one. items.title: Our cutouts had the right alpha and the wrong colors: a 0.5154 fringe score, and the fix
items.summary: For a while our in-browser background remover looked fine on a white page and bad on everything else. Pasted onto a dark background, a beach photo kept a pale rim, and a green-grass photo kept a green one. The mask wasn't the problem. The colors were. The model outputs a low-resolution alpha matte (768x768 at the time). We stretched it back to the original size with canvas bilinear scaling and applied it with destination-in. That had two side effects. Soft edges. A 4000px photo with a 768px mask means the mask is upscaled about 5x, so every edge turns into a gradient. Color fringe. A semi-transparent edge pixel is a blend: I = alpha*F + (1-alpha)*B. We changed alpha but left I as it was, so the old background B stayed baked into the edge. You can't see the second one until you move the cutout onto a new background. I defined a fringe score: inside the semi-transparent band, project the output foreground color onto the direction (local background color minus local foreground color). 0 means pure foreground color; 1 means it is entirely background color. items.title: CVE-2026-129955 & 129952: NodePress Ships With a Default Password AND a Default JWT Key
items.summary: Two CVSS 9.8s landed in NodePress 8.5.1 this week — and they’re completely independent. That’s the part worth paying attention to. CVE-2026-129955 is a default credentials flaw (CWE-1392). The admin account falls back to the password root when NP_ADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD is unset. Base64-encode it, POST it to /admin/login, get an admin token. CVE-2026-129952 is a default cryptographic key flaw (CWE-1394). The JWT signing secret falls back to nodepress-secret when NP_AUTH_JWT_SECRET is unset. Sign your own HS256 token with the default issuer, audience, and role: admin. Done — no login endpoint touched, no rate limit applies, nothing in your auth logs. Why both matter together: fixing CVE-2026-129955 (setting the password env var) closes the login path and leaves the token path open. Operators who patch one and check the box have half a fix. Two companion CVEs in the same disclosure: CVE-2026-129953 — rate-limit bypass via spoofed X-Forwarded-For (trustProxy enabled) The fix: NodePress 8.5.2 removes both fallbacks. items.title: UPC Check Digits: The One-Digit Lie That Still Scans Perfectly
items.summary: A UPC-A barcode can be perfectly valid and completely wrong for your product. Those are not opposites. They are the same bug wearing a very convincing disguise. The last digit of a 12-digit UPC-A is not a serial number and it is not a sanity check against GS1's database. It is just arithmetic. If you change one digit in the payload and recompute the check digit, the new barcode is mathematically valid. A scanner will happily read it. Your inventory system will happily file it under the wrong coffee mug. Take the first 11 digits. Multiply digits in positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 by 3. Add the even-position digits. Find the number that brings the total to the next multiple of 10. function upcCheckDigit(eleven) { let sum = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 11; i++) { sum += Number(eleven[i]) * (i % 2 === 0 ? 3 : 1); } return String((10 - (sum % 10)) % 10); } For 03600029145, that produces 2, so the complete code is 036000291452. EAN-13 flips the weights: odd positions ×1, even positions ×3. This is why copying a UPC routine into an EAN form and changing only the expected length is such an effective way to manufacture bad labels at scale. items.title: I built a daily check-in app so no parent goes unnoticed
items.summary: There's a thought that shows up once your parents start getting older and living on their own: if something happened, how long before anyone knew? It showed up for me, and it wouldn't leave. So I built the thing I wanted my own family to have. HereForYou is a small web app for a senior living alone: Once a day, they tap one big button: "I'm OK" If they go quiet, the app waits a window the family chose — 4, 12, 24 or 48 hours — then texts a family member to check on them Medication reminders, doctor's appointments and notes in one place A companion chat for the quiet hours It's free and live: https://hereforyou-15v2.onrender.com The technical detail that keeps me up at night isn't a feature — it's hosting. The app runs on a free tier, and free tiers sleep. For a CRUD app that's a shrug. For an app whose whole purpose is noticing silence, a sleeping server is the failure mode. The silence window is only as trustworthy as the thing watching the clock. So I'm raising money — for always-on servers, for the SMS alerts, and for the next two features on the roadmap: a portal where doctors can message their patients, and a one-press emergency button. items.title: Practical Handling of Webhook Task Retries After Failure in Delayed Queue Node.js Systems
items.summary: Short answer: handle failed webhook task retries with a durable event record, delayed exponential backoff, a leased worker, and receiver-side idempotency. Treat delivery as at-least-once, then make duplicate attempts harmless. A failed webhook task needs two separate decisions: when to try again, and how to make a repeated attempt harmless. The queue can provide at-least-once work delivery. It cannot make the receiver idempotent for you. My default design is a durable delivery record, exponential backoff with a cap, a lease around each attempt, and a dead-letter boundary after a small fixed number of failures. The sender records the event ID before it sends. The receiver treats that ID as a deduplication key. This keeps the delivery guarantee explicit: no silent loss, and duplicates are possible but controlled. The revenue-per-hour test matters here. I want the smallest mechanism that can explain every retry in a log and recover without a manual database edit. I ship weekly, so I outsource undifferentiated queue plumbing to a standard queue or a small internal worker. I keep the delivery state and idempotency rules in my application. items.title: Large Document Uploads: Multipart Retention for Private Object Storage Explained
items.summary: Choose multipart upload for the 1GB end of a document pipeline, and keep single-request PUT for ordinary PDFs and office files around 100MB. The deciding constraint is retention: a support-training archive needs a reproducible delete record, not just a successful upload. That sounds obvious until a mobile agent loses Wi-Fi at 87% of a ZIP. A retry of one part is cheap. A retry of the whole object is not. Start with two buckets of work. A 4MB PDF or a 30MB DOCX is usually faster to ship with one PUT. A 100MB scan can go either way, depending on the client network. A 1GB ZIP should be treated as multipart work because individual parts can be retried without throwing away completed bytes. For customer-support training artifacts, I use an application row before I touch storage. It contains tenant_id, document_id, original filename, MIME type, object key, retention deadline, and an upload status. The object key is deterministic enough to audit, such as tenant_42/training/doc_9f2/manual.zip. The database owns policy; the bucket owns bytes. items.title: Login endpoints with no attempt limit: what coding agents skip and how to catch it
items.summary: Unlimited password guessing in agent-written backends usually comes down to a login route that does exactly what the prompt asked. It looks up the email, compares the hash, returns a token, and passes every test you thought to write. Nothing in it stops someone from guessing passwords against one account as fast as the server answers. Here's a typical login handler (Express, trimmed). As far as it goes, it's correct: app.post("/login", async (req, res) => { const { email, password } = req.body; const user = await db.users.findByEmail(email); if (!user || !(await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash))) { return res.status(401).json({ error: "Invalid credentials" }); } res.json({ token: signToken(user.id) }); }); The happy path works, the wrong-password path returns a 401, and a reviewer skimming the diff sees clean code. items.title: "Proof of use" as a requirement for open source contributions?
items.summary: As an open source maintainer, I get a lot of AI slop PRs. Some of these have genuine value. Most address edge cases that almost never occur in real life. It's not that they're not fixing real problems, it's that they're fixing problems that nobody is ever likely to encounter. I'm experimenting with "proof of use" as a requirement for submissions. Specifically, you need to show me that your project that depends on my project before I'll look at your PR. "Proof of use" can be an existing open source project that imports mine (show me the git history!) or a clear description starting with "in our closed source project in production, we found that...". The specific problem that I want to address is ensuring that contributions from people genuinely depending on my software are handled, while filtering out the OpenClaw/Github green square farming/drive-by LLM noise. TechCrunch reports: Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." items.title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
items.summary: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. items.title: Checking every number an LLM writes against the source file
items.summary: LabChure turns uploaded documents (PDF, PPTX, DOCX, HWP, images and more) into a web brochure with its own URL. Getting the model to write the page was the easy part. Numbers were the hard part. A model that rewrites a spec sheet will sometimes turn "12 kW" into "15 kW", and the page still reads fine. So we added a gate. Before a page can be published, code checks its numbers against the uploaded files. Numbers with a unit: mm, kg, kWh, Hz, rpm, °C, %, inch and similar Prices: ₩ $ € ¥ £, or amounts with KRW / USD Both sides are normalized first: Unicode NFKC, lowercase, no spaces, no thousands separators. So "1,200 mm" and "1200mm" are the same token. Matching has two steps: The passage that section cites If it's not there, every file you uploaded The page goes to "needs review" and the publish API returns 409. The editor shows the token: Not found in your documents: 15 kW. You fix the text or press "Publish anyway". Nothing passes silently. After an AI edit, the check runs again on its own. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. items.title: Why We Decoupled Clients from Orders: Architecture Lessons from Building a SaaS Portal
items.summary: When building an MVP, speed is everything. You take shortcuts, design flat schemas, and ship as fast as possible. In our early iterations of ClientStatus - a platform designed to provide lightweight, zero-login project and order tracking portals for clients - we made a classic architectural assumption: 1 Client = 1 Portal / Order. It seemed clean at the time: a business creates a "client", sets a status, shares a private token link, and syncs updates via Google Sheets. Within a month of real usage, that assumption completely broke down. Here is how it failed, why we had to decouple our core domain model, and the lessons learned along the way. items.title: SpaceX Catches Starship On the First Try
items.summary: Over the weekend, SpaceX successfully caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit for the first time, demonstrating a key piece of its plan for a fully and rapidly reusable launch system. The achievement means SpaceX has now demonstrated tower catches of both Starship stages, though not yet on the same flight. "Many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)," noted SpaceX's Elon Musk. The Register reports: Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. items.title: Why I built a live request-flow visualizer for ASP.NET Core (and what v0.4.0 adds)
items.summary: Every time a request misbehaves somewhere deep inside a layered ASP.NET Core API, I hit the same wall. I know something went wrong between the controller and the database, but I don't know where, not without attaching a debugger or stitching it together from logs after the fact. That's the gap NetApiFlow is trying to close. It's an open source NuGet package that shows, live, the exact path an HTTP request takes through your own code: Controller or Endpoint, then Handler, then Services, then Repositories, then SQL. Duration per step, where a failure started, what got slow, what never ran at all. No external infrastructure. No second dashboard to deploy, no collector to babysit, no extra Docker container sitting around just for observability. The dashboard itself is an Angular app embedded straight into the NuGet package, served by your own API process. Install it, add two lines, open a URL: builder.Services.AddNetApiFlow(); builder.Services.AddNetApiFlowDashboard(); // ... app.UseNetApiFlowDashboard(); // mounted at /flow by default A request comes in and the graph lights up node by node as each step runs. If something fails, you see exactly where, with the real exception attached.

items.title: Invoice PDFs in a Multi-Tenant Backend: Who Can Download What, and Where the Edges Are
items.summary: An invoice PDF looks trivial until you add tenants, customers, and drafts. Then every download is an access-control decision. Here is how we handle it in StoreFlux, and where the edges are. There are two download routes. Staff use the admin route, and customers use the storefront route for their own orders. Both run the same query handler. The handler resolves the invoice first. For an order, it looks up the invoice that belongs to that order and the current tenant. If no invoice exists, the answer is not found, because there is nothing to render. Then it checks ownership. A super admin can read across tenants. Everyone else must match the invoice's tenant, or the request throws an unauthorized tenant error. A customer gets one more rule. They can only open invoices where the invoice's user is them, and a draft is never shown to a customer. For anyone else, the handler returns nothing, which becomes a not-found response. We chose not-found over forbidden on purpose, because a forbidden answer would confirm that the invoice exists. items.title: White-Label iOS Architecture: One Codebase, Many Brands
items.summary: Most articles about white-label mobile apps stop at “use build configurations for your colors.” That advice survives about three brands. The problems that decide whether a white-label program is maintainable show up somewhere around the eighth: release trains that no longer fit in a sprint, a test matrix nobody can run, and feature code slowly filling with the name of one particular brand. This is a structural guide to shipping one Swift codebase as many branded apps: what belongs in configuration, what belongs in code, how the Xcode project is wired, and which decisions are expensive to reverse once you have store listings in production. items.summary: I run a small file converter, imageconvert.art. Like most side projects, I wanted to know one thing: are real people using it? I didn't want Google Analytics (cookie banner, a third-party script on every page, data I don't need). So I wrote a tiny page-view counter of my own. On the first day it said I had visitors. Lots of them. Most of them, it turned out, weren't people. Here's how I fixed it with five small checks. No cookies, no fingerprinting, nothing stored that identifies anyone. Count a view every time the server renders a page. items.title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
items.summary: A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees: No internet connection. Please try again. They switch to another app, which works. Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis. A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding. A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure. The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code. Think of an API operation as several stages: Establish a usable network connection. Resolve the destination hostname when needed. Establish the secure connection. Exchange the HTTP request and response. Interpret the response body. This is a debugging model, not a claim that every request creates a new connection or performs a fresh DNS lookup. Connections and lookup results can be reused. The point is that failures at different stages need different handling. items.title: ULA Vulcan Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites
items.summary: United Launch Alliance's new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket "malfunctioned while climbing into space yesterday," writes Engadget, "destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites..." Launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the company formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. items.title: Supabase email sign-in and a profiles table for iOS, done safely
items.summary: Almost every iOS app I start needs the same first hour of work: email sign-in, a place to keep per-user data, and a way to make sure users can only touch their own rows. Supabase gives you most of it. The part people get wrong is the profiles table, because the obvious version is also the insecure one. This post walks through the setup I use: the SQL, the Swift, and the three mistakes to avoid. It assumes you know basic SwiftUI and have a free Supabase project. Supabase Auth stores credentials in auth.users. You don't add your own columns there. Instead you create a public.profiles table whose primary key is the auth user's id: create table if not exists public.profiles ( id uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade, email text, full_name text, avatar_url text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); on delete cascade matters: when the auth user is deleted, the profile goes with it. No orphans. The key in your app is public. Anyone can extract it. So the key is not your security. Row Level Security (RLS) is. alter table public.profiles enable row level security; -- signed-out clients get nothing revoke all

This guide is for the developer who published the app, not for someone seeing a Gatekeeper warning. A cracked copy can appear on a warez site, a torrent index or GitHub without showing up in your analytics. Start with a search, not a download. items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.
